cards.front: Define average velocity and provide its formula.
cards.back:
Average velocity is the total displacement ($\Delta \vec{r}$) divided by the total time interval ($\Delta t$) over which the displacement occurred. It represents the overall rate of change of position.
Formula: $\vec{v}_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t} = \frac{\vec{r}_f - \vec{r}_i}{t_f - t_i}$.

cards.front: Define instantaneous velocity and provide its formula.
cards.back:
Instantaneous velocity is the velocity of an object at a specific moment in time. It describes how fast an object is moving and in what direction at that precise instant.
Formula: $\vec{v}(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt}$.

cards.front: On a position-time graph, what does the slope of a secant line between two points represent?
cards.back: The slope of a secant line connecting two points $(\vec{r}_1, t_1)$ and $(\vec{r}_2, t_2)$ on a position-time graph represents the **average velocity** over the time interval $\Delta t = t_2 - t_1$. It is given by $\frac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t}$.

cards.front: On a position-time graph, what does the slope of the tangent line at a specific point represent?
cards.back: The slope of the tangent line at a specific point $(\vec{r}(t), t)$ on a position-time graph represents the **instantaneous velocity** at that exact moment in time $t$. It is given by $\frac{d\vec{r}}{dt}$.

cards.front: A car travels 100 km North in 2 hours, then 50 km South in 1 hour. What is its average velocity for the entire trip?
cards.back:
Total displacement: $\Delta \vec{r} = (100 \text{ km North}) + (50 \text{ km South}) = 100 \text{ km} - 50 \text{ km} = 50 \text{ km North}$.
Total time: $\Delta t = 2 \text{ hours} + 1 \text{ hour} = 3 \text{ hours}$.
Average velocity: $\vec{v}_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t} = \frac{50 \text{ km North}}{3 \text{ hours}} \approx 16.67 \text{ km/h North}$.

cards.front: Explain the mathematical relationship between average velocity and instantaneous velocity using limits.
cards.back:
Instantaneous velocity $\vec{v}(t)$ is the limit of the average velocity as the time interval $\Delta t$ approaches zero.
$$ \vec{v}(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\vec{r}(t + \Delta t) - \vec{r}(t)}{\Delta t} $$
This limit is the definition of the derivative of the position vector $\vec{r}(t)$ with respect to time $t$, i.e., $\vec{v}(t) = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt}$.

cards.front: Can an object have zero average velocity but non-zero instantaneous velocity at various points? Provide an example.
cards.back:
Yes. If an object starts at a certain position, moves, and then returns to its *exact starting position*, its total displacement ($\Delta \vec{r}$) will be zero. Consequently, its average velocity ($\vec{v}_{avg} = \frac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t}$) will be zero, even though its instantaneous velocity was non-zero throughout most of the journey.
Example: A car driving around a race track and finishing exactly where it started.

cards.front: When are average velocity and instantaneous velocity numerically equal for a moving object?
cards.back: Average velocity and instantaneous velocity are numerically equal (and in the same direction) when an object moves with **constant velocity** (i.e., constant speed in a constant direction). In this specific case, the position-time graph is a straight line, and the slope of any secant line is equal to the slope of the tangent line at any point.
